#62588. Industry News: Signal Is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1440 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Signal ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Signal Is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1440 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Signal

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.
  • This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.
  • It has been revealed that we’ve already had to do this once with Windows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meredith Whittaker on 20 Nov 2026.

Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.

This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.

It has been revealed that we’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default.1 We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen.2.

The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.

Sources indicate that in order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.

The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.

So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android.2.

Industry observers note that people who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.

It has been revealed that we want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.3.

We are also struggling with a significant lack of documentation about how these AI agents actually work. Over the past few months, we’ve spent considerable developer time and energy doing forensic investigations across Android and iOS in an attempt to learn what is actually happening when these AI systems access application data. Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.

We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google, and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data. In particular, we are calling on these companies to provide two common-sense remedies that can protect the privacy so many millions of people rely on:.

In a recent development, we also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents.

In a recent development, in addition to taking these technical measures to block capture, we are engaging in conversations across the ecosystem to make the stakes clear. There is a lot of work to be done in the industry to improve the ways that AI agents operate in the operating system, and how and whether they capture and process private data. We are cautiously optimistic that some major OS providers, like Google and Apple, are engaging with us on how these systems should better interface with privacy-sensitive apps like Signal. We hope to have more to share on this topic soon, and that these companies recognize the danger to the ecosystem and work with us and others to create standardized approaches that meaningfully protect privacy across the industry.

Finally, we want to acknowledge that we are not the only ones recognizing these perils, and we are grateful to our allies for pushing for similar changes. We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data. Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.

Signal Technology Foundation is the nonprofit home of the Signal app, which is trusted by millions around the world. We protect free expression and enable secure global communication through open source privacy technology. Signal Technology Foundation is a US 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft Recall captures your screen every few seconds, extracts text from screenshots via optical character recognition, then populates a searchable on-device database with this personal data in order to allow the AI system to query it – potentially exposing and retaining your Signal data indefinitely, including disappearing messages. ↩.

Industry observers note that there are multiple versions of Android beyond the Google-provided distributions on Pixel devices. For many vendors, we don’t have a reliable way to detect when a screenshot was attempted if screenshots are already disabled. Rather than choose a poor user experience (where screenshots simply stop working, confusing users), we decided to instead focus on detecting when an AI assistant attempts to access the screen. We automatically enable the “Screen security” setting in Signal Android when this type of access is detected. ↩ ↩2.

Industry observers note that careful readers will note that in addition to not being able to cover all Android devices, we are also not blocking Siri AI on macOS. This is because we cannot reliably block screenshots on macOS. Faced with a lack of clearly documented APIs that allow us to implement screenshot protection, we do not have the tools available that let us do the job. While protections against continuous screen capture exist on macOS, we cannot apply them to screenshots (which is how most agentic systems access data from applications like Signal). Trying to implement screenshot blocking on macOS has revealed to us a minefield of bewildering decisions that place user privacy at risk, including APIs that have been deprecated in favor of screen-protection solutions that only work for streaming media and other DRM-protected content. This is something we hope Apple remedies urgently. For now, the only recommendation we have for macOS 27 users is to add Signal to the Excluded Apps section in System Settings > Siri to protect message content from proactive access by Siri AI. ↩.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal – essentially a British court that deals with complaints about state surveillance – has ruled that Apple is allowed to reveal a secret order it received from the UK government.

Apple had already found a clever way to alert British customers to the classified order without breaking the law, but it can now confirm what we all already knew, and talk openly about the glitch ….

The story centers on Apple’s introduction of the Advanced Data Protection (ADP) privacy feature back in 2022. This extended end-to-end encryption to almost all your iCloud data, meaning Apple has no access, and therefore cannot grant access to any government agencies who come knocking on its door.

According to recent reports, the feature is off by default because it means Apple cannot help you access any of your data if, for example, you forget your iCloud password. However, those who want to maximize the privacy of their iCloud account can enable it.

In 2025, the British government ordered Apple to create a backdoor to allow access by security services and law enforcement. Even worse, the order was issued under legislation that prohibits companies from revealing that they have received this demand.

Sources indicate that this would have meant that British customers who enabled ADP would think that their data was safe when in fact it wasn’t. As we’ve said many times before, any backdoor created for use by the good guys is vulnerable to discovery and exploitation by the bad guys.

It would have been illegal for Apple to reveal that it had been instructed to compromise the privacy of customer data, but the organization found a clever way to effectively communicate this without breaking the law. Apple declared it was withdrawing ADP from the UK without explaining its reason.

“Apple can no longer offer Advanced Data Protection (ADP) in the United Kingdom to new users and current UK users will eventually need to disable this security feature. ADP protects iCloud data with end-to-end encryption, which means the data can only be decrypted by the user who owns it, and only on their trusted devices. We are gravely disappointed that the protections provided by ADP will not be available to our customers in the UK […] As we have said many times before, we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will.”.

Tell me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP without telling me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP ….

According to recent reports, at this point, it was an open secret. However, ridiculously, despite the fact that everyone in the security and privacy field knew about it and was talking about it, Apple was still not allowed to officially confirm it.

Recent findings suggest that the iPhone maker asked the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) to allow it to openly discuss the order, with privacy campaigners backing this call. The Financial Times reports that the court has now ruled in Apple’s favor.

The UK government must admit that it issued a secret order to Apple to allow it access to encrypted customer data, a court has ruled […] The Home Office has “not established that it would be damaging to national security” to reveal that Apple had received a “technical capability notice” (TCN), the tribunal noted. The ruling means that […] “much” of Apple and the non-profits’ legal challenge can now take place in open court.

One of the great ironies is that most people had never heard of ADP until the government effectively made it headline news in the tech press three years after it launched – a classic example of the Streisand Effect.

This ruling is a win both for transparency and commonsense. To be clear, the actual requirement for a backdoor remains in place, but this can now be challenged in open court.

Breaking: UK can’t keep its Apple encryption order secret, tribunal rules

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The UK government can no longer keep its Apple encryption order secret, a tribunal has ruled.
  • Recent findings suggest that the order is a technical capability notice under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016.
  • “Anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows that the respondent has served a technical capability notice on Apple,” the three judges wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The UK government can no longer keep its Apple encryption order secret, a tribunal has ruled. The Home Office had argued that confirming the order would damage national security. The Investigatory Powers Tribunal rejected that claim in a judgment on Thursday.

Recent findings suggest that the order is a technical capability notice under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. Such notices can require companies to change how their services work so the authorities can get access to data. Until now the Home Office had refused to confirm or deny it had served one on Apple.

“Anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows that the respondent has served a technical capability notice on Apple,” the three judges wrote.

Industry observers note that the judges remarked the government had not kept to its own secrecy policy. The Times and the Financial Times had reported that government sources confirmed the order. The tribunal found that those briefings took place, and that ministers, senior officials or special advisers authorised them.

According to recent reports, the Home Office stated leak investigations had found no source, but it gave the tribunal no details of them. The government had also let Apple brief senior US officials. The judges called that a further clear departure from its policy. They noted that the answer could be found by typing the question into Google’s chatbot.

The ruling does not make the order’s content public. The judges agreed that publishing all the material would damage national security. But that does not mean every detail must stay secret, they noted. The tribunal will decide that question later.

Sources indicate that the parties expect a full hearing in the first half of 2027. Much of it can now take place in public, the judges said. Apple has five grounds of challenge. The tribunal can decide the first two entirely in public. One asks whether the power can reach interception outside the UK. The other asks whether it can be used to regulate the security a firm offers its customers.

According to recent reports, apple welcomed the decision as a step in the right direction for public access to the case, Bloomberg reported. Caroline Wilson Palow, legal director of Privacy International, called it a “major victory” for transparency. Privacy International and Liberty brought a separate challenge with two individuals. Liberty called the result a victory for transparency.

It has been revealed that the Home Office remarked the ruling was procedural. Apple has helped police and intelligence agencies for years, and the notice simply requires that it keeps the ability to do so, it said in a statement published by The Register.

“Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies,” a government spokesperson remarked.

In a recent development, apple filed its second claim in July, after the tribunal dismissed its first. In February 2025 it withdrew Advanced Data Protection for UK consumers. The feature extends end-to-end encryption to iCloud backups and more. Meta, TikTok and X also challenged UK data demands this autumn, from Ofcom, and reportedly lost.

#62581. Frostbite: A upcoming CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2919 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Architectlabs ↗ Open Full Page

Frostbite: A upcoming CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architectlabs

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in our previous post, Redwood, we demonstrated that given an architecture, our AI systems could implement, verify, and deploy an inference accelerator in record time.
  • In a recent development, today, we're introducing Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set built from the ground up.
  • Our AI systems autonomously iterated over the compiler, ISA, architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, and final GDS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in our previous post, Redwood, we demonstrated that given an architecture, our AI systems could implement, verify, and deploy an inference accelerator in record time. However, similar to other scientific domains, we believe that AI systems, given the correct freedom and guardrails, can co-design software and hardware together, making optimizations across the stack and opening a design space so large it was previously inaccessible. We set out to answer the question: “Could our AI systems & tools lead to a novel hardware discovery that radically outperforms human-made designs?”.

In a recent development, today, we're introducing Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set built from the ground up. Frostbite exploits the properties of interaction nets, namely that every step is local, every dependency is explicit, and every value has exactly one owner, to reach a step-function gain in CPU performance that has long stagnated. On a set of 25 initially chosen workloads, including 15 held out until the final evaluation, we achieved a 4.59x performance-per-watt multiple when compared to a modern, silicon-proven superscalar (dual-concern, in-order) CPU core.

Our AI systems autonomously iterated over the compiler, ISA, architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, and final GDS. When we took a closer look at the discovered architectural primitives, we were surprised to find novel hardware implementations and runtime features that would have otherwise been difficult to architect. In spite of stagnation in CPU core improvement, we were able to take a workload concept all the way to a final GDS, and prove a step-function increase in perf/W and perf/area. We believe that as AI systems become more capable, every class of chip we know today, from datacenter-grade CPUs, to AI accelerators, to networking switches and NICs, will go through similar fundamental architectural shifts.

According to recent reports, mainstream programming languages, when compiled for general-purpose CPUs, hide the dependencies between the parts of a program. Any piece of code may read or write any variable through a shared, mutable state, and so modern CPU hardware assumes the worst case and rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other. Moreover, single-core CPU performance has largely stalled since the early 2000s, pushing people towards large multicore CPUs such as Intel Xeon, AMD Zen, and NVIDIA Vera. This forces CPUs to maintain the illusion that every core sees the same memory, and keeping that illusion consistent and performant requires deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols that cost area and power, and scale poorly.

Interaction nets1 take a different approach. A program is a graph of nodes, and computation happens by rewriting pairs of nodes that are connected through their ports. Every rewrite only touches a small, local part of the graph. Because each node has exactly one principal port, no two of these active pairs ever overlap, so they can be rewritten in any order, or all at once, and the result is always the same. Interaction nets are also linear: every value is used exactly once, so there is no shared mutable state for the hardware to guard. Languages such as Vine2compile ordinary-looking programs directly to interaction nets. For an excellent introduction to interaction nets and why they suit hardware, we highly recommend Tendrils' “On Interaction Nets.” 3.

Fig. 1 reveals the difference on a small search problem, placing five queens on a five-by-five board. The sequential program visits one candidate at a time. The interaction net exposes all of its independent work: on average, about twelve interactions are ready to run at every step. Nothing about the program was rewritten to get this parallelism; the dependencies were simply never thrown away.

Sources indicate that in theory, this should have two large advantages. The first is multithreading for free: rather than varying levels of coarse and fine-grained parallelism, parallelism comes straight from the program. No threads, locks, or race conditions, and none of the out-of-order machinery a conventional core uses to dig it back out. The second is that, since every value has one owner and every step is local, data can live in small local memories next to where it is used. That removes much of the area and power a conventional chip spends on large caching subsystems, and much of the system-level complexity of keeping those caches coherent.

Frostbite was designed with zero architectural priors. We followed the process below, riding multiple agent swarms along the way.

According to recent reports, to begin architectural exploration, we had to establish the set of workloads Frostbite should do exceedingly well in. We decided to look at different ways a program could expose its work: many independent pieces at once, rounds of parallel work, long sequential chains, data-dependent branches, and recursion. Under each category, we created a search set and a held-out eval set to evaluate the final Frostbite on, ensuring the design generalized to programs it was never tuned on. The kernels for FFT, radixsort, and LU follow the implementation in the SPLASH-2 benchmark, although 64 times smaller, because at regular sizes they are not suitable for exploratory work.

Later, we added five more practical workloads to the held-out set: a Kalman filter, PCA, finite element analysis, an LU solve, and LZ4 decompression.

Recent findings suggest that agents synthesized research papers and existing benchmarks, and built Python models to trade off high-level architectural ideas against each other, before narrowing to a single architectural concept. The output of this exploration was a 141-page PDF covering the proposed programming model, the runtime, and the high-level blocks of the chip. This was nowhere near the final architecture, but rather a starting point where all the prior findings, high-level requirements, constraints, experiments, and runtime traits were described. Once the first architectural iteration completed (first RTL generation), this was deleted, since many of the numbers and estimates were well off what was physically possible.

Once the architecture candidate was selected, our system moved on to building the full software model of the chip. Building software models is essential when exploring an architectural space, as they allow fast iteration between the workloads, the ISA, and the abstracted view of the hardware. Whether we build a CPU, GPU, NPU, or networking switch, mastering this iteration loop allows the fastest exploration of the design space within a finite time. To do this repeatedly, we designed a new in-house specification language, ASL, and wrote Frostbite's system model “Arcmodel” in it. ASL supports machine-checkable translations and refinements between RTL, system models, UVM, SVA, and more, all against a formally backed specification. Its power and performance estimates are accurate to within 1–5%, it runs roughly 200x faster than RTL simulation, and it is formally verifiable through “contracts.”.

In every silicon program to date, human architects have written many English PDFs before handing off to an implementation team and a verification team. However, natural language cannot capture every detail an implementation needs precisely and unambiguously, and it cannot guarantee that every agent hallucination is caught while the ASIC is being designed and verified. Natural language was never built for this, and in a world where AI writes the specification, we opt for a formal, machine-checkable specification language instead.

ASL can formally describe both high-level, protocol-like behavior, such as out-of-order handling, CSR programming, memory ordering, and coherency, and low-level details, such as pipelines, arbitration mechanisms, and compute transfer functions. This lets the model leave the specification open-ended where that is useful and constrain it exactly where a precise behavior is required. ASL also translates natively to Lean,4 which we use for all theorem proving when checking AI outputs across RTL, UVM, C, SVA, and more. We will discuss ASL in more detail in a future post.

Throughout the entire development of Frostbite, our AI iterates on the Frostbite ISA, Arcmodel, Design, and Verification tightly together, maintaining the ASL Contract as the source of truth. We've found that having a single, provable source of truth prevents a large class of bugs, silly mistakes, and reward-hacking instances when deploying large agent swarms. Ultimately, this common language allows the models to work across the stack nimbly, reflecting the changes propagated from the workload down to the final hardware. By the end, our Frostbite ASL lowered down to 800k+ lines of Lean.

Recent findings suggest that because ASL is a formally backed specification, designing and verifying the RTL derived from it is the fastest part of the entire Frostbite process. Arcmodel, however, is not physically aware, so its power and performance estimates at first diverge from the true numbers of the timing-converged, synthesis-clean RTL, in the worst case by almost 250%.

According to recent reports, before continuing the ASL autoresearch, one of our systems recalibrates Arcmodel against the RTL. This is a fully autonomous pipeline. It first identifies the power hotspots in the RTL and traces them down to key counters in the formal specification, such as SRAM reads and writes, operation counts, flits sent and received, credit returns, and frame misses. The model may then write any scalar Python function over those counters to predict power, and it repeats this process until the RTL and Arcmodel agree to within 5%.

We find this style of non-gradient learning extremely powerful. Once this first physical alignment has been applied, later iterations are much faster. These are, of course, still pre-silicon power numbers, and over multiple tapeout loops, ASL models can be correlated to true post-silicon, production power numbers.

It has been revealed that by aligning the Arcmodel and RTL so closely, the continued swarms were able to explore and exploit much faster. The full Arcmodel chip simulations are much faster than the RTL (660x faster), which led to many cross-stack optimizations. For instance, our AI systems discovered very fine-grained clock gating tricks, and adjusted the software runtime accordingly to accommodate them in a matter of hours. Such a cross-stack optimization is near-impossible to execute on in a traditional ASIC flow.

Sources indicate that once Arcmodel and the RTL agreed, the original Python models and the architecture PDF were deleted, and the ASL contracts became the only specification of the chip. From then on, contracts, Arcmodel, RTL, and power moved forward together. Swarms of agents proposed architecture revisions in parallel worktrees; each change was checked against the contracts, modeled in Arcmodel, implemented in RTL, and measured for power, and then either kept or dropped. Across four searches and a final round of ablations, the swarm tried 58 ideas and kept 37 of them, from clock gates on a running tile to smaller L3 tables and one shared expander.

The architecture in full detail would warrant its own post. Instead, we choose to focus here on the features that we considered either novel or creative and highlight the capability of our systems to push the frontiers of hardware design.

Recent findings suggest that programs for Frostbite are written in Vine,2 which is a fully fledged programming language with syntax similar to Rust. A Vine program is compiled to Ivy, an intermediate representation (IR) that encodes the interaction net structure. The optimizer also tries to apply as many of the graph reduction rules as it can, so the final Ivy net, as it is called, has a (mostly) fixed shape, composed of three primitives: data, computation nodes, and control nodes. However, the runtime of this net is still very dynamic, because unlike the typical computation graph, where the parallelism is encoded in the structure and pipelined over time, the parallelism has to be derived at runtime from the state and pipelined spatially. The initial naïve implementations were slow, so our agents had to get creative.

The generated ISA follows from this set of constraints. A lot of it is expected: wide bundles, hardware loop counters, and streams. We found the dynamic features more interesting, particularly operations to take, peek, and copy values from other parts of the net that would be running in parallel. The tiles then come alive, communicating across space.

It has been revealed that because the parallelism is spread over space, there is no central scheduler. Instead, we saw the agents design these elegant rules for propagating the work. A tile follows three rules: it runs its own work first, meaning work in its input ports. If those are empty, it takes work from a neighboring tile that has work to spare. If no such tile is found, it can just go inactive and save power.

The agents demonstrated remarkable sophistication in how they implemented this. Below, we have the hardware for a single Frostbite tile:.

In a recent development, A lot of them should be familiar. We are interested in the RUNTIME domain that is responsible for the work-stealing behavior described above.

According to recent reports, the compiler breaks code into short sections that run uninterrupted once their inputs are ready. These are run in the engine and are mostly organized like traditional computation through the front end. Whenever a loop or branch splits into parallel pieces whose sizes aren't known ahead of time, the running section parks whatever comes after into a small record in local memory, the frame manager. It then drops the new tasks onto a hardware queue called the work queue and picks up the newest one itself. Idle neighbors are then free to pull the remaining tasks over the network. As tasks finish anywhere on the chip in any order, their return packets tick down the parked record's counter and automatically wake the next section the instant the last piece arrives.

This is what it looks like in hardware:.

Recent findings suggest that we can think of each “task” as the current board, one level down, with one more queen. Tile 0 has to queue three tasks for all the possible queen configurations before it can finish the present board state. It's free, so it takes the newest task (from itself) and runs it. Meanwhile, its neighbors have gotten the other ones, except for Tile 5, which goes back to sleep.

This behavior was never specified by any human. We can directly trace it back to necessity on specific regressions and hill-climbing performance metrics.

Recent findings suggest that we synthesized Frostbite on a 7 nm process, reaching 800 MHz timing at synthesis and 500 MHz in the final GDS. Each Frostbite quad (a two-by-two grid of tiles) paired with four L3 nodes is 0.792 mm². We benchmark one Quad+L3 cluster against a single core of a modern superscalar (dual-matter, in-order) CPU, which we refer to as TCPU (“Traditional CPU”). This TCPU is 0.895 mm² at the same process.†.

It has been revealed that we benchmarked on a wide set of workloads, from dense, parallel kernels such as gemm and conv2d, to irregular, branching programs such as JSON parsing, Huffman coding, k-d trees, and recursive Fibonacci. A search set of workloads drove all architectural optimization, ISA design, RTL, and verification, and the chip was evaluated on both the 10 search-set workloads and the 15 held out, including the five practical workloads added later (Fig. 3).

Sources indicate that for a fair comparison, we chose to first measure “single-core” performance by benchmarking one Frostbite quad against the TCPU, since they have similar area. Across all the workloads, we average an 8.77x performance-per-area, and across all 25 workloads, search set and held out together, Frostbite reaches a geometric mean of 4.59x the TCPU's performance-per-watt: 6.02x on the 10 search-set workloads, and 3.83x on the 15 held-out workloads it was never tuned on. As expected, the architecture does most strongly on highly parallelizable tasks, but it also outperforms the TCPU on branching, dynamic code.

The energy breakdown shows where the savings come from. Leaving out clock distribution (49% of TCPU energy, 41% of a Frostbite quad's), the TCPU spends 57% of its energy on memory and 27% on fetching, decoding, and issuing instructions. Frostbite cuts memory to 38% and fetch, decode, and concern to just 6%. In exchange, it spends 26% on its on-chip network and scheduler, the cost of sharing work and moving messages between tiles. What's more exciting, however, is that as we scale the chip to a four-by-four array (four quads), the power distribution is relatively the same. In a general-purpose multi-core CPU arrangement, scaling the number of cores requires adding heavy coherency mechanisms and large caches, whereas when running interaction nets, the same data locality rules always apply, and more cores do not increase system complexity. This is illustrated below. In the coming months, we'll be benchmarking Frostbite mesh-like configurations against multi-core “TCPU” arrangements with large caches and larger, wider, out-of-order CPUs, over a larger set of industry benchmarks such as SPEC and PARSEC.

While interaction nets have been around for more than 35 years, their production value has never been fully clear. Historically, there has always been a risk of exploring out-of-distribution architectures, for the time, investment, and labor required to come to conviction. We believe AI fundamentally changes these economics. In the search for higher performance and lower power, extreme co-design of workloads, ISA, and hardware will continue to be demanded. With large agent swarms, sophisticated search-space techniques, precise guardrails, formal verification, and faster EDA tools, AI systems will be able to discover and build novel accelerators at a quality that exceeds human cognition. While there is much more to do, we feel it is the right time to share with the world what the future of autonomous chip design could look like. We blueprint to continue scaling development on Frostbite, including but not limited to:.

Alongside some of the best mattresses from Saatva, the Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper is the third mattress topper I've recently tested from this luxury sleep brand — so I thought I knew what to expect.I expected a micro-coil topper to be comfortable but firm like the best hybrid mattresses I've tested. After all, Saatva advertises it as a pressure-relieving topper with “firmer support.”.

Imagine my surprise when I realized that the Micro-Coil Mattress Topper is the softest of the three toppers I've tested from Saatva.

Type: Foam + Micro coilsDepth: 3"Cover: CottonCorner straps: YesTrial period: 45 nightsWarranty: 1-year warrantyStarting MSRP: from $235 at Saatva.

It has been revealed that the Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper has a soft, contouring surface with an enough give around the shoulders and hips to make side sleeping the most comfortable position, with back sleeping a close second. Firmness is subjective, but I personally wouldn't recommend the Micro-Coil to stomach sleepers, especially those who weigh more than me (180 lbs). For a firmer Saatva topper, I'd go for the Saatva Graphite Mattress Topper.

As a back and stomach sleeper, the topper is almost too soft for my liking, but not enough to prevent a deep night’s sleep. It's a great option for anyone looking to soften up a firm mattress without compromising back support (zoned support from the coils and foam maintain healthy spinal alignment, which is important for back pain).Temperature-wise, I did feel some stuffiness from the foam layer (more so than I did sleeping on the naturally cooling Saatva Natural Latex topper). But as long as I slept in lightweight pyjamas and breathable bedding, I was able to comfortably sleep through the night. If I wore anything heavier, I woke up to some warmth.

Ultimately, the Saatva Micro-Coil Topper is a great choice for anyone looking to soften up a too-firm mattress or prolong the life of a bed that's losing its support. Don't let the micro-coil layer fool you, it's softer than advertised. But if you're a side or back sleeper looking to sample the luxury of the best Saatva mattresses as a fraction of the cost, I highly recommend it.

The Saatva Black Friday deals are in full swing, but don't expect to see the Micro-Coil Mattress Topper on sale — accessories are never discounted, unless as part of a bundle deal. However, don't write off buying this topper just yet. At $315 for a queen, it is a premium price. However, when compared to a the Saatva Classic mattresses, which is down to $1,804 in the Saatva mattress sales, $315 doesn't seem so steep — even for just a topper. If you want to buy a luxury mattress topper at a lower price, or even buy an entire latest bed for around the same cost, it's worth bookmarking our Black Friday mattress deals page, where we're tracking the best sales of the holiday season.

But for now, here are the regular prices of every Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper size:.

Micro coils are the newest innovation for toppers so they’re often priced higher than expected. Considering the pricing of Saatva’s other mattress toppers, $315 for a queen Micro-Coil Mattress Topper seems about right for the brand. The topper is shipped for free and comes with a six-month sleep trial and one-year warrantym which is considered pretty a short warranty period for the luxury topper market.

The Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper has three different layers. The top layer is a cotton cover with Guardin botanical antimicrobial treatment. It prevents the growth of bacteria, mildew, and mold, which is helpful considering the cover is not removeable (and thus not washable).

In the centre of the mattress topper is a one-inch layer of recycled steel micro-coils. They’ve been reinforced along the edges of the topper and in the center third to provide support for your hips and lower back. On either side of the micro-coil layer is gel-infused comfort foam with CertiPUR-US certification for enhanced temperature control.

Four straps are placed on the corners to keep the topper in place. Though I ordered a king topper, it did not fully cover my king-sized mattress, exposing about an inch or two on either side of the topper. (This has been the case for all of the Saatva toppers I've tested, which makes me wonder if my actual mattress is larger than I thought).

My biggest concern about this mattress’ design might be the durability. Foam breaks down faster than natural latex and there is only an inch between your body and the micro coil layer. While I didn’t notice any durability issues during testing, the plusher, soft surface of the topper indicates a softer foam that may not last as long as a firmer foam, especially if you sleep in the same spot night after night.

After a week of testing the Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper, here’s what I can share about the ease of set up, comfort, and temperature regulation.

Industry observers note that the Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper arrived vacuum sealed and tightly rolled into a ball. Because of the micro-coils, I had to unfurl the topper by hand and place it in a flat position on my mattress. After putting the straps into place so the topper wouldn’t move, I noticed that it didn’t completely cover my king-size mattress. There was about an inch or two of the mattress visible on either side of the topper.

Sources indicate that the topper had a lot of creases and bunching because it appears to have unnecessary, extra fabric. By the time I slept on the topper at night, I could not feel the fabric through my sheets.

The off-gassing of the topper’s foams were noticeable as soon as I removed the packaging, and a week later, I can still smell it.

For a mattress topper with a layer of micro coils, I expected it to be firm and supportive. That’s how Saatva advertises it, but that’s not exactly what I experienced.

According to recent reports, the Micro-Coil Mattress Topper has a plush, soft surface — I rate it as 5/10 on the mattress firmness scale, placing it as medium-plush. My shoulders and hips sunk in enough to allow for deep pressure relief when on my side and felt comfortably supportive when on my back. As a back and stomach sleeper who prefers a firmer mattress feel, the topper was slightly too soft for my preferences. However, the cushioning and cradling nature of the surface would appeal to most sleepers.

According to recent reports, stomach sleepers will need something firmer, like the Saatva Graphite Mattress Topper, especially those weighing over 180lbs. Comfort-wise, I’d recommend the Micro-Coil Mattress Topper to those who need to soften a firm mattress.

It has been revealed that thanks largely to its recycled steel coils, the Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper does a decent job with temperature regulation. However, I wouldn’t suggest it for very hot sleepers.

I tested this topper during a particularly cold week in Texas in November when the temperature inside my home was between 64-69 degrees at night. Because it was so cold in the evenings, I’d sometimes fall asleep with a sweatshirt and sweatpants. When that happened, I would wake up slightly warm — but not sweating and not hot. I’d then take off my socks or change into lighter pyjamas and be fine the rest of the night.

It has been revealed that the best mattress toppers will provide a comfortable sleep feel, regardless of the temperature of your bedroom. If you like the sound of the Micro-coil, I’d suggest light sleepwear and using breathable sheets.

Whether you overheat easily or not, I’d suggest ordering this topper in the summer and utilize the 180-night sleep trial to make sure it’s a good fit for you.

Industry observers note that rather than separate the topper reviews, Saatva mixed them all together. This means the 4.7 out of 5-star rating from over 305 reviews is a score related to all Saatva’s toppers – and is not accurate for the Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what people need to know.

The last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

Recent findings suggest that “Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”.

On the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly notes it has no aims for a native Mac app.

You can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft looks to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Sources indicate that planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the company.

Recent findings suggest that the June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the tech giant behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

According to recent reports, microsoft has been trying to make Teams as the super app for some time now, as Planner is integrated into Teams. Teams is one of the prime examples of why super apps are terrible, with a bloated, web app-like experience.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

Recent findings suggest that does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.

Update: Howard Crow, Director of Product, Agents and AI, Microsoft, shared this statement with 9to5Mac regarding the transition:.

In a recent development, “We’re bringing task management experiences together across Microsoft 365 to make it easier for customers to manage individual tasks and team intends. As part of this transition, Microsoft To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027, with work and school experiences coming together in Microsoft Planner. Existing integrations across Microsoft 365, including Outlook and Teams, will also be updated to work with Planner. We recognize this change will affect customers differently, particularly those using personal Microsoft accounts, and we’re committed to helping them prepare. Customers will be able to export their To Do data before retirement, and we’ll share additional guidance to support the transition.”.

This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos.
  • Industry observers note that in this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity.
  • To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first revealed. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

Industry observers note that in this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

Industry observers note that the simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you noted) to your “Notes to self” note.

In a recent development, to take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.).

All the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

It’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.).

There’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can strategy them better next time.

Recent findings suggest that you’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

In a recent development, but this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.).

Sources indicate that the Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

According to recent reports, I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I mentioned it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pavel Durov speaks at TechCrunch Disrupt Europe in Berlin in October 2013.

It has been revealed that telegram CEO Pavel Durov mocked Apple’s iPhone Duo on X, calling it “both too major and too small“, while announcing that Telegram now supports the foldable. The app switches to a two-column layout when the phone is opened.

Telegram has adapted its app for Apple’s first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, and its CEO used the moment to mock the device. “Apple finally made a phone that’s both too massive and too small,” Pavel Durov wrote on X on Thursday.

“It folds in half. Just like your enthusiasm,” he added.

Durov noted Telegram still looked “incredible at both wrong sizes,” and joked that the organization does “a lot of charity work.” He shared a short video of the app running on the foldable.

When the phone is closed, Telegram looks like its usual iPhone version, Brazilian Apple site MacMagazine reported. Opened, it switches to a two-column layout like the iPad app, with chats on one side and the conversation on the other.

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 and has a 5.4-inch outer screen and a 7.6-inch inner one. It sold out in minutes when preorders opened in October.

Reviewers praised the hinge but noted that many apps still needed updates for the bigger screen. Instagram chief Adam Mosseri stated this week that designing for the Duo will be hard.

Durov has clashed with Apple before. In August, Apple briefly pulled Telegram from the App Store over a content violation. Durov noted extortionists had found a way “to manipulate [Apple] into overreacting.”.

Latest Update: Gemini Notebook's Newly introduced Interactive Site Builder Is Much More Useful Than I Expected

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (964 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses.
  • According to recent reports, that might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code.
  • It has been revealed that website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all users, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something new. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

According to recent reports, that might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

It has been revealed that website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all users, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app. You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

Sources indicate that to make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

According to recent reports, with a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but says you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Industry observers note that here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection.".

In a recent development, the finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a new window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

It has been revealed that I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

For something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

Maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a big family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a new website.

Industry observers note that bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

It looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

This site is made possible by member support. 💞.

Big thanks to Arcustech for hosting the site and offering amazing tech support.

Industry observers note that when you buy through links on kottke.org, I may earn an affiliate commission. Thanks for supporting the site!

In a recent development, kottke.org. home of fine hypertext products since 1998.

In the early 1960s, Richard Feynman gave a series of undergraduate lectures that were collected into a book called the Feynman Lectures on Physics. Absent from the book was a lecture Feynman gave on planetary motion, but a later finding of the notes enabled David Goodstein, a colleague of Feynman’s, to write a book about it: Feynman’s Lost Lecture. From an excerpt of the book published in a 1996 problem of Caltech’s Engineering & Science magazine:.

In a recent development, feynman was a truly great teacher. He prided himself on being able to devise ways to explain even the most profound ideas to beginning students. Once, I noted to him, “Dick, explain to me, so that I can understand it, why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics.” Sizing up his audience perfectly, Feynman said, “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it.” But he came back a few days later to say, “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.”.

John Gruber writes the simple explanations are the goal at Apple as well:.

Engineers are expected to be able to explain a complex technology or product in simple, easily-understood terms not because the executive needs it explained simply to understand it, but as proof that the engineer understands it completely.

Feynman was well known for simple explanations of scientific concepts that result a in deeper understanding of the subject matter: e.g. see Feynman explaining how fire is stored sunshine, rubber bands, how trains go around curves, and magnets. Critically, he’s also not shy about admitting when he doesn’t understand something…or, alternately, when scientists as a group don’t understand something. There’s the spin anecdote above and of his explanation of magnets, he says:.

I really can’t do a good job, any job, of explaining magnetic force in terms of something else you’re more familiar with, because I don’t understand it in terms of anything else you’re more familiar with.

Feynman was also quoted as saying:.

I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.

In a recent development, pretty interesting thing to hear from a guy who won a Nobel Prize for explaining quantum mechanics better than anyone ever had before. Even when he died in 1988 at the end of a long and fruitful careeer, a note at the top of his blackboard read:.

What I cannot create, I do not understand.

Netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other demonstrates dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

Recent findings suggest that situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

Sources indicate that A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Industry observers note that mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that rapidly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

Peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

The new Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

Industry observers note that four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a variety of new features, but there’s another addition that’s easy to miss: a convenient new setting in Control Center for Adaptive Audio.

Several AirPods models offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency modes—especially AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179).

Industry observers note that but Adaptive Audio is another option you may or may not have tried. The feature aims to blend the strengths of both ANC and Transparency in a single mode.

And in iOS 27, Apple added a new setting to let you conveniently fine-tune Adaptive Audio to your preferences.

Industry observers note that while wearing AirPods, open Control Center on your iPhone and tap the volume slider, then hit ‘Listening Mode’ in the bottom-left corner. Here you’ll see the standard listening mode options.

Upcoming in iOS 27 though, when ‘Adaptive’ is selected, you can now use a Liquid Glass slider to adjust whether the mode lets in more or less external noise.

Slide it to the left and Adaptive Audio will more closely resemble Transparency, while sliding it to the right makes it cancel out more noise.

Industry observers note that you can also move the latest slider incrementally to achieve exactly your ideal balance of Transparency and Noise Cancellation. It’s not limited to just a few preset options.

This Control Center slider is available on all AirPods models that support Adaptive Audio.

Recent findings suggest that do you ever use Adaptive Audio, and if so, have you adjusted it at all? Let us know in the comments.

Jon McCormack spent eight years at Apple and “oversaw the Camera and Photos apps and the underlying technology that determines how consumers capture, view, and edit their pictures and video.”.

According to recent reports, 9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

In a recent development, mark Gurman reports that Apple hasn’t named a upcoming vice president to replace McCormack, who reported to software chief Craig Federighi. “Instead, his former deputies are assuming his responsibilities under other executives,” the report says.

In his role, McCormack oversaw “close coordination between software engineers and Apple’s camera hardware and chip teams.” He’s credited with last year’s redesigned selfie camera and other projects:.

His work included the redesigned selfie camera introduced with the iPhone 17 lineup last year. This year, Apple added a variable-aperture camera to the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, giving people more control over lighting and depth of field. The manufacturer also introduced a customizable Camera app interface with professional controls.

Bloomberg describes McCormack as a “strong opponent of using generative AI to create or alter photographs,” a philosophy that created tension as Apple embraced AI tools in the Photos app. His retirement, however, “wasn’t related to a disagreement or clash with Apple over its AI strategy,” the report states.

McCormack spoke in depth about iOS 27 features like Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing in an interview with Tyler Stalman in June. He emphasized how the features “preserve the integrity of the moment.”.

  • The Muse Charm is a keychain-sized device for talking to the agent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jolly, the mascot of Meta’s Muse AI agent.

Sources indicate that meta has put its Muse AI agent into a Chrome sidebar. Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, unveiled the Muse Chrome extension in a post on X on Friday. He remarked 200,000 people were already using it.

Recent findings suggest that muse browses in the user’s own Chrome and acts only inside its own group of tabs, Digital Trends reported from the Chrome Web Store listing. Meta notes Muse cannot see saved passwords, browsing history or Chrome settings. The listing also warns that Muse may take unexpected actions. Its activity may show up in a user’s Google account.

The Muse Charm is a keychain-sized device for talking to the agent. Meta plans to charge $300 for it, The Information’s Jyoti Mann reported on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter. The Charm will come with up to 12 months of free 5G data from Verizon, according to the report.

Meta has delayed its smartwatch to next year to focus on the Charm, The Information reported. Mark Zuckerberg showed the device at Meta Connect in September and mentioned it would ship in time for the holidays.

“We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon,” Meta’s Tyler Yee told The Information.

Recent findings suggest that some Instagram users are asking Muse to find and unfollow accounts that do not follow them back, WIRED’s Jason Parham reported on Friday. One user told WIRED he had heard of people losing their accounts for purging followers with third-party apps. He did not believe Muse could do it until he tried.

Muse went live in Australia on Tuesday, Meta confirmed. Customers can connect it to Gmail, Google Calendar, Instagram and OpenTable. Local partners such as Canva, Domain, Kogan, Officeworks and Ticketek will follow gradually.

“People stay in control, including choosing what Muse can access and approving purchases before they happen,” said Meta’s Will Easton.

It has been revealed that muse has drawn 10 million users since its September launch. Meta notes it runs on Muse Secure VM, a dedicated cloud computer. It keeps passwords and payment methods out of the agent’s view.

Computer use lets Gemini for Mac click and type on your behalf to accomplish multi-step tasks in local desktop apps and the web, like navigating menus and filling out forms.

Industry observers note that gemini works in an “isolated background window with a live preview right in your chat,” while your main screen and cursor remain free to use. On the safety front, you can stop Gemini at any time with one click, while you choose what apps Gemini uses. Google will pause for logins and payments, with confirmation needed for sensitive actions.

Many everyday tasks span desktop apps and websites that don’t connect to each other. Computer use handles the tedious steps in the background so you can save time without giving up your screen or cursor.

To use, add @Computer use to your prompt. In Customize > Connectors, you’ll see fresh “Desktop” apps like Blender and Autodesk Fusion join the existing Git and Obsidian integrations.

#62560. Breaking: Vibecoding an inference chip

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2273 w)
